analysis.one_liner: Restores looser eligibility rules for coal miners' black lung disability benefits and forgives past benefit repayments.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 1990 with 24 cosponsors, the bill was referred to a House subcommittee and died without ever receiving a vote before Congress adjourned in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it much easier for coal miners with at least ten years in the mines to qualify for federal black lung benefits, which are paid to miners disabled by coal dust in their lungs. Miners with claims filed between mid-1973 and early 1980 would have been presumed disabled if they produced even one piece of qualifying medical evidence, such as a single positive chest X-ray, unless the coal operator could prove otherwise. It also would have forced a fresh review of old denied claims under the more generous pre-1977 rules, barred the government from clawing back benefits paid for more than two years even if a claimant was later ruled ineligible, and given claimants' lawyers a set contingency fee of up to 25%. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners with ten or more years of mining employment whose claims were filed between July 1973 and April 1980, along with their survivors. These miners had filed claims under an 'interim presumption' system that later court and agency decisions narrowed; the bill would have restored that system for them. It also would have reopened old denied claims for review under the more generous standards in effect before the 1977 reform law, and protected anyone who had received benefits for two or more years from having to pay them back.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Long-tenured coal miners and their survivors

how_it_helps.text: A miner with at least ten years of coal mining employment whose claim was filed between July 1973 and April 1980 would be presumed totally disabled by black lung disease if any single piece of qualifying medical evidence was presented — one positive X-ray, one set of positive breathing tests, one set of positive blood-gas tests, or a physician's documented opinion.
Other medical evidence could be used only to try to rebut the presumption, not to defeat the claim at the start, and the claimant would not need to meet any heightened evidentiary standard.

The Secretary of Labor would have to re-review claims filed before April 1, 1980 (or under the older part of the program at any time) that were still pending or had been denied, applying the criteria in effect before the 1977 reform law, with approved claims paid immediately and retroactively.
If a claimant received benefits for at least two years before a final denial, those benefits could not be treated as an overpayment, and claimants already forced to repay would get their money back.

The bill established a contingency-fee system letting claimants hire lawyers on a no-win, no-fee basis, capped at 25% of benefits paid during the period of representation, which made legal help affordable for disabled miners.

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators and the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, which pays claims where no responsible operator can be found and is financed by an excise tax on coal. Looser presumptions and re-reviewed old claims would have increased benefit liability charged to the fund and to operators contesting claims. The federal Treasury's interest payments on advances to the trust fund would also have been suspended through fiscal 1995, which shifts a cost away from the fund.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal operators and the industry-financed trust fund

drawbacks.text: Re-reviewing every claim filed before April 1980 — including ones already denied decades earlier — would have imposed a large administrative workload and added retroactive benefit costs to the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, which is funded by a tax on coal production.

The bill would have allowed benefits to be granted on a single positive X-ray or blood-gas test, with other medical evidence considered only in rebuttal; critics of such presumptions argue that a single abnormal reading can reflect disease unrelated to mining, so some awards would go to people disabled by other causes.

Prohibiting repayment of benefits paid for two or more years, even after a final determination of ineligibility, removes a safeguard against mistaken or fraudulent payments and puts that cost on the fund and the Treasury.
The 25% contingency-fee arrangement means a share of disabled miners' benefits would go to attorneys rather than the miners and their families.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill was a repair job: Congress had originally ordered a generous interim presumption for black lung claims, later decisions narrowed it, and long-tenured miners who had filed during that window were left with denied claims under stricter rules. The fiscal cost — higher trust fund liabilities and forgone Treasury interest — is real but modest relative to the program, and the no-repayment and fee provisions are the weakest parts, since they transfer some of the cost of errors to the fund and trim miners' own awards. On balance the bill would have shifted money and odds toward a narrow group of severely sick workers and their widows at the expense of the coal industry.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee referred it to its Labor Standards subcommittee two days after it was introduced, nothing ever came of it, and Congress adjourned with the bill still stuck there.

narrative.text: Rep. Austin J. Murphy of Pennsylvania introduced the Black Lung Benefits Restoration Act on August 3, 1990, joined as an original cosponsor by 24 other House members.
All 25 original sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, drawn mostly from coal-mining states such as Pennsylvania, Kentucky, West Virginia, and Ohio.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the day it was introduced.

On September 4, 1990, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, where it remained; the full action history shows no markup, no vote, and no further action before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators and the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, whose benefit liabilities would have grown under the bill's looser standards, are better off that it died. The miners and survivors with old denied claims received no relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal operators and the trust fund

sides.party_line_note: All 25 original sponsors were House Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but no vote was ever held, so the opposition's partisan shape never showed on the record.

industries.note: A single-piece-of-evidence presumption plus re-review of decades-old denied claims would have sharply raised the odds that disabled miners' claims were approved, increasing benefit liability charged to operators and to the trust fund they finance through excise taxes. Operators benefit from the stricter standards that had been in place.

The fund would pay for the expanded claims reviews and looser presumptions, but Title IV extends its moratorium on interest owed to the Treasury through fiscal 1995, saving it substantial interest costs. The fund is financed by a coal-industry excise tax, so its costs fall largely on that industry.
The bill creates a contingency-fee system capped at 25% of benefits paid, giving disabled miners an affordable way to hire counsel and giving claimant-side lawyers a defined payment stream.
